claims.claim: Didymus the Blind (c. 313 – c. 398) was a Christian theologian and biblical exegete from Alexandria, Egypt.
Didymus became blind at the age of four, before he had learned to read.
Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, appointed Didymus head of the school at Alexandria.
Didymus remained a layman all his life.
Didymus was heavily influenced by Origen and was a loyal follower of his teachings.
Didymus was one of the principal opponents of Arianism and staunchly defended the doctrine of the Trinity.
The Second Council of Constantinople in 553 condemned the works of Didymus, along with those of Origen and Evagrius Ponticus, though not his person.
Because of this condemnation, most of Didymus's works were not copied during the European Middle Ages and were subsequently lost.
Only one scholium on Hebrews is attributed to Didymus the Blind in the Greek catena tradition.
The fragment on Hebrews survives as part of the catena tradition, where extracts from various church fathers were compiled into collections of scholia on biblical books.
Didymus had the same attitude as Clement of Alexandria regarding the Epistle to the Hebrews, not presenting it as written by Paul.
